title: Sum Digits Until One Is Left
statement:
Take a non-negative integer num. Replace it with the sum of its decimal digits, and keep doing that until a single digit remains. Return that digit.

Try to do it without any loop or recursion.

examples.why: 5 + 9 = 14, then 1 + 4 = 5. One pass is not enough.
Already a single digit, so nothing changes.

hints: Just simulate it first. How many rounds can a 10-digit number need?
Adding up the digits does not change the remainder when you divide by 9, because 10 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9.
So the final digit is num mod 9, except that a positive multiple of 9 ends at 9, and 0 stays 0.

explain.intuition:
Write num as d₀ + d₁·10 + d₂·100 + …. Every power of 10 is 1 more than a multiple of 9, so modulo 9 that sum is just d₀ + d₁ + d₂ + …. Summing the digits keeps the remainder mod 9 unchanged, round after round.

The process ends at a single digit with that same remainder. For a positive number the digit is 1 to 9, so remainder 0 means the digit is 9. Only num = 0 ends at 0. Together: 1 + (num − 1) mod 9 for positive numbers.
steps: Otherwise return 1 + (num − 1) % 9, which maps remainders 1..8 to themselves and 0 to 9.
pitfalls: Returning num % 9 directly: 900 gives 0, but the answer is 9.
Forgetting that 0 is valid input and must return 0, not 9.
Summing digits only once: 59 becomes 14, which still has two digits.

solutions.title: Simulate
solutions.idea: Sum the digits repeatedly while the number has more than one digit.

solutions.title: Digital root formula
solutions.idea: Digit sums keep the remainder mod 9, so the answer is 1 + (num − 1) mod 9 for positive num.

followups: Do the same in base 16. What replaces 9?
Use the same remainder fact to check a long multiplication by hand (casting out nines). Which mistakes does it miss?
